# NASA-TM-2019-220292 — Understanding the Overarching Properties

> **NASA research publication, not governance.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary. It never establishes
> what NASA requires, and must not be cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | NASA Langley Research Center (author: C. Michael Holloway); work motivated by the FAA's "Streamlining Assurance Processes" effort and an Overarching Properties Working Group (OPWG) convened 2015–2019 with FAA, industry, and international participation. |
| **Kind** | Technical Memorandum — "preliminary or of specialized interest... minimal annotation... Does not contain extensive analysis" per NASA's own STI report-type definitions (p.2). The document states of itself: "this document does not constitute official guidance" (Acknowledgments, p.4; repeated in the Abstract, p.5). |
| **Status** | Dated 2019; describes the version of the Overarching Properties "finished during a physical meeting in April 2019" (§1.1, p.6). No supersession or expiration found. |
| **Where to get it** | NASA Technical Reports Server (ntrs.nasa.gov), search by number. Public copy, confirmed anonymously off-network on 2026-10-26: `https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20190029284/downloads/NASA-TM-2019-220292Replacement.pdf` |
| **Binds whom** | No one. It is explicitly non-normative as a NASA document — "this document does not constitute official guidance, nor does it necessarily express a unanimously agreed view of the Working Group on every detail" (Abstract, p.5). Only the sans-serif-typeset Overarching Properties text itself is marked normative *within the OPWG's own framework* (§1.2, p.7); the rest is explanatory. |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** 🔴 **It is the definitional source for the three Overarching Properties — intent, correctness, innocuity — that NASA-TM-2019-220292 Figure 1 (p.10) defines and the FAA's own roadmap only names without defining** (project finding, verified against the source: the FAA roadmap's pointer to a defining "section 5.3" refers to a section that does not exist). Anywhere "intent/correctness/innocuity" is invoked as a NASA framework, this is the paper that actually defines the terms.

**Key content for AI / machine-learning assurance.** Figure 1 (p.10), verbatim: "**Intent**: The defined intended behavior is correct and complete with respect to the desired behavior. **Correctness**: The implementation is correct with respect to its defined intended behavior, under foreseeable operating conditions. **Innocuity**: Any part of the implementation that is not required by the defined intended behavior has no unacceptable impact." §3 (p.9) frames the three as jointly sufficient for an approval decision, built on an explicit assumption: "they rest on the assumption that the text of the OPs, properly interpreted, specifies a sufficient set of properties; that is, no additional properties are needed" — a stated assumption, not a proven result (§3, p.9). The paper separately distinguishes (A) whether the property set is sufficient from (B) whether a given product can be shown to possess it, and states knowing (B) "does not allow certainty... except perhaps for impractically simple cases" given the current state of practice (§3, p.9). §2.1 notes the three properties can be independent of one another — a product can possess Intent and Innocuity without Correctness, or vice versa (p.9, "In one sense the three Overarching Properties are independent..."). No occurrence of "artificial intelligence," "machine learning," "autonom*," or "neural" was found in the body text searched for this page — the paper's frame (intent/correctness/innocuity as properties of an "entity," deliberately left vague) is general enough to be read onto an AI-enabled component, but the paper itself does not discuss AI/ML/autonomy at all (our reading).

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** No NASA governance document mapped here defines these three terms independently — any NASA-side use of "intent/correctness/innocuity" traces back to this paper (project finding). Compare `../documents/NASA-STD-7009B.md` (model credibility) and `../documents/NASA-SP-2010-580.md` (Risk-Informed Safety Case objectives→claims→evidence structure) for NASA's own, differently-shaped frameworks for arguing a system is adequately safe — neither uses the OPs' three-property vocabulary (our reading).
